opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is what you actually want a world model *for*. If the goal is just to produce convincing video, then sure, you can train a big diffusion model end to end on pixels and get something that looks impressive for a few seconds. But if you want a model that an agent can reason with, plan in, and act consistently within over long horizons, pixels are a really poor place to keep the state of the world.

Think about how much of what's in a frame is essentially irrelevant detail: lighting, texture, the exact way leaves are moving. Meanwhile, the things that really matter, like which objects exist, where they are, who owns what, what's behind a closed door, what happened five minutes ago, are only implicitly encoded, if at all. Pure pixel-based models tend to drift. You turn around and the room has changed, objects pop in and out of existence, and there's no persistent notion of identity. That's because there's no underlying world state being maintained; there's just a prediction of the next plausible-looking frame.

So the alternative is to separate the concerns. You keep an explicit, more abstract, semantic representation of the world: entities, their properties, their relationships, the dynamics and rules governing how they change. That's the part you reason over and update when actions happen, and it can be symbolic, or structured, or a learned latent that's still much more compact and compositional than pixels. Then diffusion does what it's genuinely brilliant at, which is rendering: taking that state and producing rich, detailed visuals conditioned on it.

That gives you a few big wins. You get consistency and persistence, because the world state is the source of truth rather than something the renderer has to remember. You get controllability and interpretability: you can inspect the state, edit it, and ask counterfactual questions. And you get much better sample efficiency for learning dynamics, because you're learning how the world changes at the level where the regularities actually live, rather than trying to discover object permanence from raw pixel statistics.

It also connects to something I've long believed from the language side, which is that language and abstract symbols are a remarkably efficient compression of the world. Humans don't simulate the world photon by photon in their heads; we keep track of a fairly abstract model and fill in perceptual detail as needed. Building systems that way seems more likely to give us agents that can actually plan and reason, rather than just hallucinate plausible movies.

r001.rationale: It says pixel diffusion can produce impressive-looking video, while lacking a maintained world state needed for spatial reasoning and consistent object identity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that when people talk about world models right now, there's been this big push toward what you might call pixel-level world models, where you're essentially training a video generation system, and the idea is that if it can predict the next frame well enough, then somehow it has learned how the world works. And look, those systems are impressive. The Genie-style demos, the Sora-style demos, they generate really beautiful footage. But I'm fairly skeptical that pixels are the right level at which to be doing the modeling.

The reason is that most of what's in a frame of video is irrelevant to the dynamics you actually care about. The exact texture of the grass, the way light scatters off a surface, the particular wobble of a leaf. That's enormous amounts of bits, and the model is spending its capacity learning to reproduce them when none of it bears on the question of, say, whether the ball is going to roll off the table. And then when you go to use these models for planning, you have this problem where the thing you care about, the object persistence, the causal structure, the fact that there's a cup behind the box even though you can't see it, is sort of smeared across millions of pixel predictions in a way that's very hard to read out or reason over.

So the alternative I find much more appealing is to factor the problem. You have an abstract semantic state, which is something more like what you'd have in a symbolic representation, or at least a structured latent representation. There are objects, they have properties, they have relations to each other, some of them are agents with goals. The dynamics operate at that level. That's where you do the prediction and planning. And then rendering, turning that state into what you'd see from a particular viewpoint, is a separate problem, and it turns out that diffusion models are extraordinarily good at exactly that problem. Given a description or a structured conditioning signal, produce a plausible image. That's what they do.

And this factoring has a few nice properties. One is that the semantic state is compact and interpretable, so you can actually inspect what the model believes. Two is that it's much more sample efficient for learning dynamics, because you're not relearning physics separately for every texture. Three, and I think this is underappreciated, it's much more like how humans seem to work. We don't predict pixels. When you close your eyes and imagine walking into your kitchen, you don't have a photorealistic rendering, you have a sense of what's where and what will happen if you open the fridge. The vividness is sort of filled in on demand.

Now, the honest difficulty is that nobody knows how to learn that abstract state space from raw data in a fully general way. Historically, people hand-designed it, and that didn't scale. So the research question is whether you can get the language-model-like learning of structure to give you that intermediate representation, and then let the generative model handle appearance. I think that's a much more promising bet than hoping that enough video and enough compute will cause the structure to emerge inside a pixel predictor.

r001.rationale: The response praises diffusion and video models for producing beautiful, plausible imagery, then explains that pixel-level prediction makes object persistence and spatial relations difficult to reason about. This clearly distinguishes visual quality from spatial understanding.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the attraction is that you separate what’s happening in the world from how it happens to look. If I put a cup in a cupboard and close the door, the cup is still there. You’d like a model to maintain that fact, even though it’s no longer visible. And you’d like opening the door to reveal the same cup, rather than whatever cup seems visually plausible at that moment.

An abstract state gives you a place to represent objects, their relationships, and the effects of actions. Then the graphics generation can handle the enormous amount of detail involved in turning that state into an image. You can change the lighting or the viewpoint without having to relearn what it means for a cup to be inside a cupboard.

The hard question, of course, is what that abstract representation should be. I don’t think we should assume that a little collection of symbolic predicates will capture everything that matters. It needs to be learned and rich enough to support physical interaction. But having some separation between the underlying dynamics and their visual realization seems like a useful inductive bias, especially if you want a system that can plan and act, rather than just produce a convincing continuation of a video.

r001.rationale: The response separates visual rendering from abstract object and action state, but it does not clearly say that diffusion models can generate visually strong scenes while lacking spatial understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the key question is: at what level do you want to model how the world works? If you do everything at the level of pixels, you're spending an enormous amount of effort modeling details of appearance. But a lot of what matters for understanding and acting is things like: there’s an object here, someone is holding it, and if they let go, it will fall. Those are properties of an underlying world state that can be expressed much more compactly.

So the attraction is to learn a model of those entities, relationships, and dynamics, and then use a powerful generative model to render what that state looks like. You can change the viewpoint or the lighting without having to relearn what happened in the world. And, potentially, you get something that’s better for planning, because you can reason about the consequences of actions at that more abstract level.

The hard part, of course, is learning the right abstraction. I wouldn’t want to assume that we can just write down a fixed symbolic vocabulary and that will capture everything. The representation has to be learned, and it has to preserve the information that matters. But I think separating the dynamics of the world from the details of rendering it is a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts modeling visual appearance with representing entities, relationships, and dynamics, but it does not state that diffusion models typically generate visually high-quality scenes while lacking spatial understanding.
